results.title: Michelline Syjuco finds her way back to wearable art
results.description: It was in 2008 that Michelline Syjuco fully embraced her artistic side, launching her “Armadillion” installation. It featured life-size busts and wearable art pieces so enchantingly beautiful that it became her ticket to the world. Michelline was selected by the British Fashion Council to represent the Philippines at the International Fashion Showcase at London Fashion Week in 2015. Then, she was shortlisted for Vogue Talents (Vogue Italia) and represented the country at Paris Design Week. But in the whirlwind of it all, Michelline found herself slowly losing sight of the person behind the artist. She knew that if she continued to keep up with the pace, she would eventually burn out. And she did. “It was after returning from Paris Design Week that I decided I needed to consciously take a pause. I had been running myself ragged for far too long,” Michelline recalls. “Eight years had gone by, and although I loved to be working all the time, I also felt like I was missing out on other aspects of life. Friends would invite me out, and I would always decline because of looming deadlines, and I didn’t want to neglect that aspect of my life anymore.” During her break, she found solace in painting, channeling the creativity she poured into creating wearable art into the canvas. In 2018, Michelline did a solo exhibition, opening new opportunities for her to present her work in a less demanding way. It wasn’t until COVID-19 that she had to pause once more and contemplate. This year, Michelline is marking her comeback to wearable art with an exhibition aptly titled “Return to Savant-Garde.” Here, the multidisciplinary artist and designer cannibalizes and reconstructs found materials, welding disparate elements together to produce new forms. The collection merges her childhood visits to Quiapo Church with Philippine mythology, resulting in pieces that function as contemporary “agimats” or “anting-antings.” In a conversation with Manila Bulletin Lifestyle, Michelline takes us through her creative process as she turns found objects into pieces that carry fragments of memory, mythology, and her own journey back to wearable art. Can you tell us the story behind ‘Return to Savant-Garde’? How does this exhibition capture the artist you are now? During my 10 years away from creating wearable art, I found myself increasingly doubtful about being able to come up with works as significant as the ones I had produced years before. I think every artist goes through periods of self-doubt and apprehension, especially when being away from the scene for so long. I followed my mother’s advice, which was to just put my blinders on and focus on my goals and what I wanted to create. I decided to just dive right back in and scout for materials. I’m the kind of artist that has to feel the materials in my hands before I can process and make something. Once I got my hands on these materials that I sourced from thrift shops, junkyards, antique dealers, etc., my mind began to work as it used to, figuring things out like a puzzle, and the gateway to creation was finally open again. “The Savant-Garde” was the title given to me for a magazine cover story years ago, and it just stuck with me. To be avant-garde means to be ahead of the game—a pioneer, a front-runner. And a savant is a term meaning “to be learned.” Both of these words, I feel, define who and what I am. I was never formally schooled in making jewelry; everything I learned was through trial and error. I do things my own way because that's all I know how to do. And yet, it's because of this self-taught method of creating that I am able to produce what others can't. You mentioned influences such as the ‘manananggal,’ ‘bungisngis,’ and ‘tikbalang,’ which are quite the opposite of the more enchanting beings in Philippine folklore. What draws you to them? I’ve always been drawn to the dark side of sword and sorcery, mythology, and folklore. There's just something so interesting about the characters and their origins—especially the ones we consider villainous. There's just so much depth, and every character feels like they have layers to peel back before eventually uncovering who and what they truly are. I’ve also always found myself seeing the beauty in what others consider undesirable and even grotesque. Beauty is something that exists in everything. We just need to learn how to adjust our perspective and challenge preconceived notions of what is aesthetically pleasing and what is undesirable. As an artist, that's something I feel strongly about highlighting in my work. What materials are you using for the upcoming exhibition? Are you also highlighting a particular technique? For this collection, I've used brass, silver, and gold, which are mostly finished in my signature oxidized and distressed aesthetic. I want the pieces to look like relics from another world, objects that have a history and story of their very own. I’ve also incorporated prefabricated objects that have been cannibalized and re-attached to other odds and ends in order to produce new forms. I was heavily influenced by memories of my mother and grandmother taking me to Quiapo, where I would find myself fascinated by all the “anting-antings” (talismans) for sale by the roadside. These wearable talismans were considered power objects, and my new collection draws heavily from that. I want the wearer to feel empowered because the piece speaks to them and of them to others. It's a way of saying, “This is who I am,” to a world that has become so consumed with sameness. To that, my lola would say, “Let’s dare to be different.” How would you define wearable art? Wearable art is art that just happens to be wearable. It is not defined by the stones used or the monetary value of the materials. It can literally be made out of anything. It is something one of a kind, infused with a soul of its very own. What do you hope the audience takes away after viewing your exhibition? I hope that the audience takes away a newfound appreciation for unconventional materials and that the exhibit makes them think twice about how they perceive beauty and creativity. The number one rule of creating is that there are no rules!

results.title: TREASURE ISLAND First Look Sends David Oyelowo, Hayley Atwell & Tom Sweet on a Dangerous Pirate Adventure
results.description: Pirates, buried treasure, deadly competition, and David Oyelowo as Long John Silver? Yeah, this could be a fun adaptation of Treasure Island! The first images have been released for MGM+ and Paramount+’s upcoming six-part adventure series Treasure Island, offering our first look at the new take on Robert Louis Stevenson ’s classic pirate story. The series stars Oyelowo (Silo) alongside Hayley Atwell ( Avengers: Doomsday ) as Bess Hawkins and Tom Sweet ( Great Expectations ) as Jim Hawkins. The first-look photos also feature Jack Huston ( Boardwalk Empire ) as Aaron Graham and Tomer Capone ( The Boys ) as Billy Bones, giving us an early taste of the characters who will be caught up in the hunt for Captain Flint’s legendary treasure. The story follows young Jim Hawkins and his fiercely determined mother, Bess, after they come into possession of Flint’s treasure map. That discovery throws them into a dangerous race for an unimaginable fortune, complete with pirates, competing agendas, and all the trouble you’d expect when a map promising a mountain of treasure lands in the wrong hands. Joining the main cast are Craige Els ( Andor ) as Mr. Arrow, Tristan Sturrock ( Poldark ) as Captain Smollett, and Neil Pendleton ( Outlander ) as Mr. Cameron. Treasure Island will premiere October 11 on MGM+ in the United States, followed by its Paramount+ debut in the UK and Ireland on October 12. The series comes from Robert Murphy ( Vera, Shetland ), who created the adaptation. Jeremy Lovering, William McGregor, and Paul Walker direct, with Mark Hedges serving as producer. The show is a Paramount+ original series made in association with MGM+ and Fifth Season, with Playground Entertainment producing. Paramount+ executives Sebastian Cardwell and Paul Testar commissioned the series. Stevenson’s story has been adapted countless times, but a six-episode series format gives this version plenty of room to really dig into the story and characters. More importantly, it’s a full-on pirate adventure! There simply aren’t enough of those on TV these days, and I love Pirate stories!
